newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian government seen safe amid party woes.
newsitem.headline: Indian government seen safe amid party woes.

text.p: A corruption scandal and internal dissent pose a threat to Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party, but analysts on Sunday said there was no immediate threat to the government.
"I doubt any real threat to the government. It will not affect the coalition," Rasheed Talib, an independent political analyst, told Reuters.

Earlier this week, a group within Gujral's Janata Dal party and left-wing parties joined with the Congress party, a key ally of the fractious ruling coalition, in asking for the resignation of Janata Dal party chief Laloo Prasad Yadav, who is also chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar.
Bihar's governor on Tuesday authorised the federal police to pursue legal proceedings against Yadav in a $280 million corruption scandal over animal welfare funds.
Yadav says he is innocent and has repeatedly rejected demands that he resign from either of his posts.
Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma, also accused in the scandal, resigned on Friday.
Janata Dal is the largest party in the fractious United Front coalition.
The scandal has stoked tension in Janata Dal and confronted the prime minister with his biggest political challenge since he took office in late April.
"I don't know whether the government is going to fall, but it is definitely going to be shaken up," said Mahesh Rangarajan, an analyst at the Centre for Contemporary Studies.
Gujral would face a serious threat to his authority from squabbling within his divided party if it were to splinter as a result of internal party elections, analysts said.
Laloo is locked in a party leadership tussle with challenger Sharad Yadav, no relation of the Bihar chief minister.
Mutual mistrust over party internal poll proceedings has spilled over into courtrooms.
"Even if there is any upheaval it is not going to affect the United Front government," said Atul Anjan, a senior leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI).

Talib said the coming together of the United Front and the Congress last week to jointly endorse the nomination of Vice President K.R. Narayanan as their presidential candidate in the indirect polls set for July 14, augured well for Gujral.
"Sitaram Kesri is not going to upset the government," he said.

Kesri, whose Congress party offers vital support to the United Front government, in April toppled the coalition government headed by then-prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda and renewed its support only after the front ousted Deve Gowda as leader.

Analysts said Gujral's immediate challenge was to persuade his disparate coalition partners, ranging from free-market advocates to communists, to take a decision on the crucial issue of oil prices at the next meeting of the decision-making Steering Committee scheduled for June 27.

At its last meeting on June 16, the 15-party United Front postponed a decision on whether to raise oil prices to plug the government's mounting debt owed to state oil companies for selling oil at below world market prices.
The debt was estimated at 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) at the end of March.
Left-wing parties in Gujral's alliance have strongly opposed any price increase.
